title: Medical language
subtitle: dose, side effects, a rash of, fever pitch
summary: Read a medicine leaflet with confidence, and use medical words as metaphors - an ailing economy, a rash of complaints, a jaundiced view.

lesson.heading: A medical information leaflet
lesson.text: Here is the warning section from a packet of painkillers: 'Before taking this medicine, talk to your doctor or pharmacist if you are taking **low-dose** aspirin (up to 75 mg daily), suffer from **asthma** or have a past **history** of asthma, have a connective tissue **disorder**, or have a history of **gastrointestinal disease**.'

examples.text: A **low dose** is a measured amount of medicine that is relatively small.
**Asthma** is a condition in which breathing becomes difficult because the air passages have narrowed.
Your medical **history** is the record of the conditions you have experienced.
A **disorder** is an illness of the body or mind; **gastrointestinal disease** affects the stomach or digestive passages.

lesson.heading: Risk, dose and duration
lesson.text: The leaflet continues: 'Talk to your doctor if you are **elderly**, as this increases the risk of **adverse reactions**, or if you have heart problems, have had a previous **stroke**, or think you might be at risk of these **conditions**. Do not **exceed** the stated **dose** or **duration** of treatment.'

examples.text: **Adverse reactions** are unwanted results of taking a medicine.
A **stroke** is a sudden change in blood supply to the brain, causing loss of function in part of the body.
It is important not to **exceed** the number of pills the doctor tells you to take.
Maria is not allowed to drive for the **duration** of her treatment.

lesson.heading: Side effects and warning signs
lesson.text: 'Like all medicines, these tablets may sometimes cause **side effects** - unwanted effects in addition to the intended one - though not everybody gets them. Stop taking this medicine and **seek medical help** if you suffer any **allergic reactions**, are sick and it contains blood or dark **particles**, pass blood in your **stools**, or have a **stiff neck**, headache, **nausea**, **vomiting**, fever and **disorientation**.'

examples.text: **Allergic reactions** affect the skin or breathing after contact with certain substances.
**Disorientation** - not knowing where you are - can be the result of a bang on the head.

lesson.note: If you vomit, you are sick. If you only feel like vomiting, you feel sick - that is nausea.

lesson.heading: Medical metaphors: symptoms and diagnosis
lesson.text: Social problems are often talked about as if they were illnesses. A **symptom** is a problem indicating an illness, so a social problem can be a **symptom** of something deeper, or **symptomatic of** it. Causes can be **diagnosed**, and the outlook for a situation is its **prognosis** - medically, how experts expect an illness to develop.

examples.text: The current spate of car thefts is a **symptom** of a deeper underlying problem.
This behaviour is **symptomatic of** his general lack of self-confidence.
What do you think the **prognosis** is for the peace talks?

lesson.heading: The metaphors in use
lesson.text: These are everyday journalistic English. Note that you **reach** fever pitch, you take a **jaundiced view** of something, and you have your **finger on the pulse** of public opinion.

examples.text: The economy has been **ailing** for some time, but there are hopes of a recovery soon.
There has been a **rash of** burglaries in the neighbourhood.
With a week to go before Anne's wedding, preparations had reached **fever pitch**.
Experts take a rather **jaundiced view** of the likely success of the peace talks.
I hope Helen's enthusiasm will **infect** everyone else.

lesson.text: Diagnosis looks backwards - what is wrong and why; prognosis looks forwards - what will happen next.

exercises.prompt: Anorexia is a serious eating ___ in which a person tries to eat as little as possible.
exercises.explanation: A disorder is an illness of the body or mind.

exercises.prompt: It is important not to ___ the number of pills the doctor tells you to take.
exercises.explanation: To exceed the stated dose is to take more than the amount prescribed.

exercises.prompt: Talk to your pharmacist if you suffer any ___ reactions to the tablets.
exercises.explanation: Adverse reactions are unwanted results; the parallel noun phrase is side effects.

exercises.prompt: The doctor asked me a lot of questions about my medical ___ .
exercises.explanation: Your medical history is the record of the conditions you have had - not your medical ~~story~~.

exercises.prompt: Excitement reached ___ pitch as the day of the final match dawned.
exercises.explanation: To reach fever pitch is to reach a point of very high intensity.

exercises.prompt: Although industry is doing well in the north of the country, in the south it is ___ .
exercises.explanation: An ailing industry or economy is one with a lot of problems.

exercises.prompt: The manager said that there had been a ___ of complaints about the hotel.
exercises.explanation: A rash of something is a number of similar things happening at the same time.

exercises.prompt: The problems in our neighbourhood are ___ of wider problems in society.
exercises.explanation: Something symptomatic of a problem is evidence that the problem exists.

exercises.prompt: What do you think the ___ is for the peace talks?
exercises.explanation: A prognosis is how experts expect a situation - or an illness - to develop.

exercises.prompt: I'm afraid I have rather a ___ view of the banking industry.
exercises.explanation: A jaundiced view is an unenthusiastic or sceptical one, formed by previous bad experiences.

exercises.prompt: Match each metaphor with what it means.

exercises.statement: If you feel sick, you have actually vomited.
exercises.explanation: To feel sick is nausea - wanting to vomit. If you actually vomit, you are sick.

exercises.prompt: Is each expression literal medical language, or a medical word used as a metaphor?
